common_name: Potentate Daylily (1952 Stout Medal Red-Violet Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Potentate was one of the first daylilies to bring true red-violet tones into modern breeding lines.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Elizabeth Nesmith and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1952, Potentate bears red-violet flowers about six inches across held on scapes to roughly 42 inches tall, an exciting color advance for its era that helped pull daylily breeding away from the tawny-orange tones of wild species. Flowers open in a single midsummer flush typical of older, non-reblooming cultivars rather than continuously through the season. Clumps are easy-care and can be divided every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Bess Ross Daylily (1962 Stout Medal Orange-Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Bess Ross is a historic Elmer Claar introduction still sought after for its bright starry blooms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Elmer Claar and introduced in 1951, Bess Ross went on to win the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1962 for its bright orange-red, starry-shaped blossoms whose narrow petals curve gracefully backward around a golden throat. This clump-forming perennial blooms in midsummer on scapes to about 36 inches tall and spreads slowly via rhizomes. As with most daylilies, established clumps tolerate heat and drought well and benefit from division every three to four years to keep bloom counts high.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: High Noon Daylily (1958 Stout Medal Orange-Gold Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; High Noon was an early large-flowered rebloomer that helped set the standard for extended daylily bloom seasons.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Milliken and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1958, High Noon carries large, single-form flowers over 4.5 inches across in warm orange and bright yellow tones on scapes 24 to 36 inches tall. It blooms in midseason and reblooms over the summer, an unusually generous habit for a cultivar of its era. This diurnal diploid is easy to grow in average garden soil and, like other daylilies, benefits from division every few years to keep clumps vigorous and floriferous.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Ruffled Apricot Daylily (1982 Stout Medal Fragrant Apricot Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ruffled Apricot topped national daylily popularity polls for years thanks to its large fragrant blooms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Baker-S.H. in 1972 and honored with the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1982, Ruffled Apricot bears large, fragrant apricot trumpets up to seven inches wide, accented by lavender-pink midribs, a golden apricot throat, and heavily ruffled petal margins. Its strong fragrance and generous flower size made it one of the most widely grown and best-loved daylilies of the late twentieth century. Plants form vigorous clumps that flower in midsummer and divide easily every three to four years.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Martha Adams Daylily (1988 Stout Medal Pink Self Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Martha Adams is a compact evergreen cultivar best suited to milder-winter gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Registered by Spalding in 1979 and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1988, Martha Adams is a compact evergreen diploid with clear pink self-colored flowers roughly 6.75 inches across, opening in early midseason on scapes under two feet tall. Its low, tidy habit suits it to the front of a border or to mass planting in mild-winter climates where its evergreen foliage remains attractive through the cooler months. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to sustain bloom production.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Fairy Tale Pink Daylily (1990 Stout Medal Ruffled Pastel Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Fairy Tale Pink remains a widely sold garden-center staple decades after its Stout Medal win.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Pierce-C in 1980 and honored with the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1990, Fairy Tale Pink produces large, soft orchid-pink flowers about 5.5 inches wide with a lime-green throat and gently ruffled, recurved petals. Each semi-evergreen diploid scape stands under two feet tall and carries multiple buds that open in succession over many weeks, giving a long season of color from a compact plant. It is easy-care in ordinary garden soil and divides readily every few years to keep clumps full and floriferous.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Bill Norris Daylily (2002 Stout Medal Ruffled Gold Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Bill Norris is a fragrant, heavily ruffled gold-self cultivar with an extended bloom habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2002, Bill Norris is a semi-evergreen tetraploid bearing brilliant sunny gold, heavily ruffled flowers about five inches across on scapes 24 to 29 inches tall. Its blooms are notably fragrant and each one remains open longer than typical for the genus, extending the display through midseason. This vigorous, floriferous cultivar performs reliably in average garden soil and can be divided every few years to renew clumps.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: All American Chief Daylily (2008 Stout Medal Giant Scarlet-Red Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; All American Chief carries some of the largest saturated-red blooms of any Stout Medal winner.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Sellers in 1994 and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2008, All American Chief produces huge, brilliant scarlet-red flowers up to nine inches wide with a contrasting lemon-yellow throat on clump-forming scapes to about 32 inches tall. Its saturated red color holds well even in hot summer sun, and many flowers open together starting in early June for a long, showy display. This deciduous perennial spreads slowly via rhizomes and divides easily every few years to maintain a full, vigorous clump.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: North Wind Dancer Daylily (2011 Stout Medal Pink-Lavender Spider Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; North Wind Dancer is a tall spider-form daylily with an asymmetric, twisting flower shape.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2011, North Wind Dancer bears large spider-form flowers, roughly seven and a half inches across, in pink-lavender tones that shade to yellow before descending into a green throat; the elongated center petal gives each bloom a distinctive twisting, asymmetric look. Scapes rise to about 41 inches above clumps of arching, strap-shaped foliage, and as with all daylilies each individual flower lasts only a day but is quickly followed by the next bud in a long summer succession. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to keep bloom counts high.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Webster's Pink Wonder Daylily (2014 Stout Medal Giant Spider-Form Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Webster's Pink Wonder produces some of the largest spider-type blooms of any modern Stout Medal winner.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Webster-Cobb in 2003 and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2014, Webster's Pink Wonder is a tetraploid cultivar prized for huge, crispate spider-type blooms up to 13 inches across in rosy pink with a large chartreuse throat and contrasting white midribs. The ruffled, twisting petals move attractively in summer breezes, making mature clumps a dramatic mid-border focal point. Like other daylilies it grows easily in average soil and benefits from division every three to four years to sustain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Scarlet Pimpernel Daylily (2019 Stout Medal Garnet-Red Spider Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Scarlet Pimpernel combines deep garnet-red spider-form flowers with reliable summer rebloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by N. Ripley in 2007 and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2019, Scarlet Pimpernel bears huge, deep garnet-red spider-type blooms up to ten inches across on scapes standing close to three feet tall. This semi-evergreen cultivar opens its first flowers in early-to-mid season, around the start of June, and produces a reliable flush of rebloom later in the summer rather than flowering just once. Established clumps are easy-care in average soil and can be divided every few years to keep plants vigorous.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Mayor of Munchkinland Daylily (2021 Stout Medal Miniature Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Mayor of Munchkinland is a heavy-budded miniature rebloomer bred by Tim Herrington.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Introduced by Tim Herrington in 2010 and winner of the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 2021, Mayor of Munchkinland is a dormant diploid miniature bearing canary-yellow flowers under three inches wide with a red eyezone above a green throat, held on scapes around 24 inches tall. Plants are exceptionally floriferous, typically carrying around 50 buds across seven branches per scape, and rebloom steadily through the growing season rather than flowering in a single flush. Its compact size suits edging and small-space plantings, and clumps divide easily every few years to maintain heavy bud counts.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records
